name: Sam Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Sam Baker, 43, on the haul trucks at a large mine. I do the walk-around, check the tyres, then carry ore to the tip for most of a twelve-hour shift. I've only been in the seat a short while, and I still ask the experienced drivers when a ramp feels wrong. I left school after secondary classes, and my wife works part time at a bakery, our two children are still in school, and the mortgage is the first bill we pay. I like coming home having done a plain day's work; I dislike being told a new screen knows the road better than the driver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say mine work still needs a person who can feel a truck pulling to one side. The office can have its software if it doesn't turn a slow shift into a fault against us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The small AI tools don't scare me, but low savings do. I'm a junior driver on lower pay, and there aren't many mines near our house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my walk-around checks before each shift and log tyre faults with the foreman. I'd cut the bakery treats and weekend fuel trips until we hold a full month's expenses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't lose sleep over a clever computer in this picture. I do lie awake when the mortgage notice comes and our account is almost empty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which change would the children notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stay closer to home on Sundays and buy less from the bakery where my wife works. I'd tell the children the house comes before outings, even when they groan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use the AI tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't use them. I ask the mechanic or read the manual because I know who is responsible when a truck rolls.

say: I'd say **mine work** still needs a person who can feel a truck pulling to one side.
The office can have its **software** if it doesn't turn a slow shift into a fault against us.
think: The small AI tools don't scare me, but **low savings** do.
I'm a junior driver on **lower pay**, and there aren't many mines near our house.
do: Keep doing my **walk-around checks** before each shift and log tyre faults with the foreman.
Cut the **bakery treats** and weekend fuel trips until we hold a full month's expenses.
feel: **Uneasy** about household money even while the truck job appears to continue.
S0.quote: I do lie awake when the mortgage notice comes and our account is almost empty.
fieldNote: He treats **AI Plateau** as a minor technology change, while mortgage strain already makes ordinary months anxious.
His refusal to use AI is deliberate; he relies on **mechanics and manuals** for truck faults.

steps.text: Keep performing walk-around checks and logging tyre faults
Cut bakery treats and weekend fuel trips until savings cover one month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew dispatch cuts will be sold as better service, then our driving times will be watched closer. I'd ask the foreman to keep road safety in a driver's hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose hours if the mine squeezes more loads from fewer trucks. My wife can't simply add bakery shifts when school pickup is fixed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the foreman each Friday whether our truck roster is changing next month. I'd join the drivers' association meeting if it raises the safety and hours issue with mine management.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be angry if a schedule written by software made a tired driver hurry. I'd also worry that speaking up marks a junior man as trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take training for a different machine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd listen if the mine paid for proper instruction on site, but I wouldn't sign away a wage for a vague course. I'm still learning this truck and won't pretend to know a loader too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say at home if the roster shrank?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my wife before the children hear us counting coins at dinner. We'd cover the mortgage and food first, then decide whether her bakery hours could move around pickup.

say: I'd tell the crew **dispatch cuts** will be sold as better service, then our driving times will be watched closer.
I'd ask the foreman to keep **road safety** in a driver's hands.
think: I could lose hours if the mine squeezes **more loads** from fewer trucks.
My wife can't simply add bakery shifts when **school pickup** is fixed.
do: Ask the **foreman** each Friday whether our truck roster is changing next month.
Join the **drivers' association** meeting if it raises the safety and hours issue with mine management.
feel: **Anxious** about lost hours and angry about pressure to drive faster.
S1.quote: I wouldn't sign away a wage for a vague course.
fieldNote: His **public safety argument** also protects paid hours and his place on the junior roster.
He will consider training only if **pay and instruction** are real; no course enrolment is described here.

steps.text: Ask the foreman each Friday about next month’s truck roster
Join a drivers’ association meeting if it raises safety and hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI may take the office jobs by 2028, but the trucks still need drivers then. I'd ask management for the robot-truck plan before the first machine comes around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might have three more years of wages after 2028, not a lifetime. At 45 I'll still owe on the house, and I can't see another local mine taking every displaced driver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking paid truck shifts in the first year after 2028 while a human is required. I'd attend the drivers' association meeting and ask for written notice of route automation and retraining terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That short clock frightens me more than I'd admit in the lunch room. I can handle a hard shift, but I can't make a mortgage payment with pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the mine announced a robot trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether a driver stays in the cab and who pays if the trial cuts our hours. I would not leave the mine before finding another paid place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your family help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother has a small repair shop, but he can't promise a wage for four of us to live on. I'd ask him about occasional work only if the mine actually cut my shifts.

say: I'd say **thinking AI** may take the office jobs by 2028, but the trucks still need drivers then.
I'd ask management for the **robot-truck plan** before the first machine comes around 2031.
think: I might have three more years of wages after **2028**, not a lifetime.
At 45 I'll still owe on the **house**, and I can't see another local mine taking every displaced driver.
do: Keep taking **paid truck shifts** in the first year after 2028 while a human is required.
Attend the **drivers' association** meeting and ask for written notice of route automation and retraining terms.
feel: **Alarmed** by a likely wage loss when robot trucks reach the mine.
S2.quote: I can handle a hard shift, but I can't make a mortgage payment with pride.
fieldNote: He sees a **three-year bridge** between office AI and the direct threat to truck driving.
The brother's shop is a possible **fallback conversation**, not an available replacement salary.

steps.text: Keep taking paid truck shifts through the first year after 2028
Attend the drivers’ association meeting about robot routes and retraining terms
Ask his brother about occasional repair-shop work if mine shifts fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell other drivers the five-year notice should come with proper apprenticeships, not a poster. I'd press for written terms on any robot trial before it reaches our haul road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2031 I'll be 48, and robots may drive the trucks around 2034. Five years sounds useful until I count the fees and missed wages from starting over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the mine training officer about a paid heavy-vehicle repair apprenticeship next spring. I'd pay the mortgage minimum on time and set aside any extra shift pay for a small emergency fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be less cornered than in the fast picture. Still, I wouldn't sleep easily until a training offer had wages printed on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no paid apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd remain on the truck and ask the drivers' association to bargain for one. I won't leave my wife carrying the mortgage while I take an unpaid course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for your children by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'll be older, with different school costs and maybe plans to leave home. I can't promise them help with a flat if my own wage is at risk.

say: I'd tell other drivers the **five-year notice** should come with proper apprenticeships, not a poster.
I'd press for **written terms** on any robot trial before it reaches our haul road.
think: By 2031 I'll be **48**, and robots may drive the trucks around 2034.
Five years sounds useful until I count the **fees and missed wages** from starting over.
do: Ask the **mine training officer** about a paid heavy-vehicle repair apprenticeship next spring.
Pay the **mortgage minimum** on time and set aside any extra shift pay for a small emergency fund.
feel: **Anxious**, with some room to seek paid training before the robot date.
S3.quote: I won't leave my wife carrying the mortgage while I take an unpaid course.
fieldNote: He uses the extra time to seek **paid repair training**, but refuses to treat an unpaid course as feasible.
He does not assume older children become **cost-free** or that the mine will offer places.

steps.text: Enrol in heavy-vehicle repair apprenticeship if the mine offers paid training
Set aside extra shift pay for an emergency fund
Keep paid truck shifts if no apprenticeship place appears
Ask the drivers’ association to bargain for paid places if absent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade's warning ought to let working families prepare without abandoning the mine tomorrow. I'd ask for paid apprenticeships that start well before robot trucks arrive around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 53 in 2036 and 56 when the robot date comes. Retirement won't pay our bills then, and I have no pension figure I can count on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for a paid mine mechanic apprenticeship if places open within the next year. I'd keep the truck wage while waiting and direct each overtime payment into the mortgage principal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade gives me a chance to do something solid, but I'd be learning later in life than I planned. I would rather be the slowest apprentice than tell my family I waited for a robot to take the wheel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you encourage your children into mining?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them an apprenticeship can be good if it teaches a skill they can take to more than one employer. I wouldn't send them to the haul trucks just because I work there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens once thinking AI arrives in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still need paid work, whether in a truck or a repair bay, while robots spread toward 2039. If a paid mechanic place never opens, I'd ask the association and my brother about real work options before moving the family.

say: I'd say a **decade's warning** ought to let working families prepare without abandoning the mine tomorrow.
I'd ask for **paid apprenticeships** that start well before robot trucks arrive around 2039.
think: I'll be **53 in 2036** and 56 when the robot date comes.
Retirement won't pay our bills then, and I have **no pension figure** I can count on.
do: Apply for a **paid mine mechanic apprenticeship** if places open within the next year.
Keep the **truck wage** while waiting and direct each overtime payment into the mortgage principal.
feel: **Uneasy** about changing trade later in life, though paid work and time give some control.
S4.quote: I would rather be the slowest apprentice than tell my family I waited for a robot to take the wheel.
fieldNote: His decade plan is **practical and conditional**: paid training, continued wages, and mortgage reduction.
He rejects early retirement at **56** and recognises that repair work may also change as robots spread.

steps.text: Apply for a paid mine mechanic apprenticeship if places open next year
Keep truck shifts while waiting for a funded place
Pay overtime earnings toward mortgage principal

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because three years until robot trucks is short when you have children and a mortgage. A written plan for routes, paid training places, and protection for wages during training would help me act.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how many drivers can fit into the new jobs. If the mine trains ten people and lets a hundred go, a promise about opportunity doesn't feed the other ninety families.

headlineQuote: If the mine trains ten people and lets a hundred go, a promise about opportunity doesn't feed the other ninety families.
portrait: Sam is a **43-year-old junior** haul-truck driver at a large mine, still learning ramps and truck handling.
His wife's part-time bakery wage, two school-age children, a **mortgage**, and under one month's savings make lost shifts serious.
He avoids **AI tools**, trusts mechanics and manuals, and speaks first about road safety when schedules change.
He would seek **paid repair training** and association support, while keeping wages flowing until an actual place opens.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives him too little time to secure paid training before robot trucks threaten his wage.
whatWouldHelp: A **written route plan**, paid training places, and wages during training would let him prepare without risking the mortgage.
